paras: The shooting of Ode Johnson took place in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, in mid-August 1915, when Captain George F. Lumb, assistant superintendent of the State Police, fired on Johnson, a Black man, and wounded him in the right leg as he fled from an alleged attempted assault on a woman near Lumb's home. Johnson was arrested, failed to win release on a writ of habeas corpus, and was convicted at the September quarter sessions and sentenced to six months. The Harrisburg Telegraph, the only paper found to cover the case, followed it from a weekend crime roundup through the court columns.

According to the Telegraph's first report, Johnson was accused of attempting to assault Miss Sarah Bent along the Jonestown road near Twenty-First street on a Saturday night. The alleged assault took place near Lumb's home, and Lumb "shot at the negro when he heard the woman scream for help," one shot lodging in the flesh of Johnson's right leg. Johnson fled, the city police were notified, and Policeman Wilson arrested him the next morning at Eighteenth and Walnut streets.

Later court items told the story somewhat differently. One said Lumb "captured and shot at" Johnson while he was trying to escape from the home of a neighbor of the officer in State street, and another said Johnson was "chased, fired upon and arrested" by Lumb on the night of August 11.

Johnson was given a hearing before Alderman Hoverter in the county jail on August 16. Held on charges of attempting a criminal assault upon a "colored maid" and resisting an officer, he sought release through Attorney J. R. Bennett, who petitioned Judge C. V. Henry of Lebanon, sitting for the Dauphin County judges, for a writ of habeas corpus. After the habeas corpus proceedings he was sent back to jail to await trial.

The quarter-sessions list set his case, "assault with intent to rape," for Monday, September 27. The next day the Telegraph reported that Johnson had been convicted of assaulting a "negro maid" and had received six months. No inquiry into Lumb's use of his weapon appears in the coverage.

The Harrisburg Telegraph first ran the case in the last paragraphs of a front-page story headed "Crime Wave Hits City Over Week-End," which listed holdups, two razor slashings and "a brutal attack upon a girl." Its later items appeared in the court news, with headlines built around the officer: "Negro Whom Captain Lumb Fired at Will Ask Court Tomorrow For Writ of Habeas Corpus" and "Ode Johnson, Chased by Captain Lumb, Is Returned to Prison." Throughout, the paper called Johnson "the negro," described the officer's chase as "exciting," and treated the shooting as part of the arrest without comment.
No other white paper and no Black newspaper was found reporting the case.

The Telegraph's items differ on several details: the first report dates the incident to Saturday night, August 14, while a September item gives August 11. The woman is named Sarah Bent in the first report and Sarah Henry, "a negress," later, and the officer is called Frank Lumb in one item and George F. Lumb in three. The first report, printed two days after the incident and the most detailed, has city police making the arrest, while later items credit Lumb with the capture.

reader.title: Shooting of Ode Johnson
bases: A State Police captain fired on Johnson, a Black man accused of an attempted assault, as he fled, wounding him in the leg, after which city police arrested him; no mob or crowd is reported (A2, A4, A5).
All reports come from one newspaper, the Harrisburg Telegraph, whose several items agree that Lumb fired on and wounded or chased Johnson but are not independent of one another (A2, A3, A5, A7).

accounts.label: First Telegraph report (police account)
accounts.gist: Lumb heard a woman scream near his home on the Jonestown road and shot at Johnson, hitting him in the leg; Johnson fled and city police arrested him the next morning.

accounts.label: Telegraph court news
accounts.gist: Lumb 'captured and shot at' Johnson as he tried to escape from a neighbor's home in State street a few weeks earlier, or 'chased, fired upon and arrested' him on the night of August 11.

framing.detail: The Telegraph filed the case under 'Crime Wave Hits City Over Week-End' and later court headlines ('Johnson Wants to Get Out of Prison', 'Ode Johnson, Chased by Captain Lumb, Is Returned to Prison'), calling Johnson 'the negro' and treating the shooting as part of his arrest without questioning it.

conflicts.note: The first report, printed two days later, is nearer the event; the August 11 date in a court item may be an error.
Later items agree she was a Black ('colored', 'negro') maid (A4, A7).
